name: Malcolm X
role: American Muslim minister and Black nationalist leader; founder of Muslim Mosque, Inc. and the Organization of Afro-American Unity (assassinated 1965)
summary: Malcolm X spoke for Black self-determination, community control of politics, schools and economy, and the right of armed self-defence where government failed to protect Black Americans. After leaving the Nation of Islam in March 1964 and making the Hajj he dropped its racial separatism and white-devil doctrine, built a pan-African, human-rights framed movement and spoke of racism as a global problem, while still excluding whites from membership of his organisation. His economic remarks in 1964-65 criticised capitalism and said he favoured whatever served Black people, but he proposed no economic system.

notes: Positions follow the most recent clear statements (April 1964 to February 1965). Before the break with the Nation of Islam (to March 1964) he advocated racial separation and a separate Black state; Message to the Grass Roots (Nov 1963) is used only where consistent with later statements. The Hajj letter (April 1964) shows him revising earlier views on white people; the OAAU, however, admitted only people of African descent, and Wikipedia reports he began reconsidering black nationalism in his last months. On capitalism and socialism he made late remarks that capitalism was to blame for racism and that he would favour socialism if it helped Black people (Wikipedia), but no statement in the texts opened matches a specific statement, so those are null. The Oxford Union speech (Dec 1964), 'Malcolm X Speaks', the 1965 interviews and the Autobiography could not be opened as full text, so Vietnam, women, family and several other topics are null. The OAAU program page carries no date; the OAAU charter text was read by Malcolm X at the June 1964 rally. Deepening pass (claude-opus-5-5, 2026-10-31) searched the full texts of the Autobiography and Malcolm X Speaks (Internet Archive) for line 14 themes: prisons, tokenism and gradual change, the press and educated elites, the world court, Africa as homeland, capitalism, consumption, technology, parties and leaders. The world-court remarks concern charging the US government, not leaders before criminal courts, so international-criminal-courts stays null; his remarks on the press (manipulated by the FBI and CIA) and on 'educated Negroes' do not match media-academia-power or educated-out-of-touch. No local corpus covers him (died 1965). Later pass (claude-sonnet-5-5, 2026-11-20): read the maintainer's library texts (Breitman, Perry, Pathfinder volumes, Autobiography, Claude Lewis interview) and searched them for war and intervention, revolution and violence, capitalism and socialism, reparations, land, women and marriage, courts, taxes and aid. Revolution and political violence are answered from his 1963-64 speeches, which he never repudiated; his late remarks that capitalism and racism are linked, and that socialism attracts newly independent states, state no position on a statement. Other new statements (monetary policy, constitutional design, gender, technology, environment) are not addressed in his texts and stay null. For the widest lines (pluralism/authoritarianism, regulated economy/laissez-faire, leader and party, nation first) the library texts were searched for dictatorship, one-party rule, the press, private property, free enterprise, tariffs and self-sufficiency, Nkrumah, Nasser and Castro; he defended African leaders the West called dictators but took no position on a leader bypassing gridlock, one-party rule or economic systems, so those stay null.

power-shapes-accepted-knowledge.rationale: In January 1965 he said the racial categories 'were put together by anthropologists who were nothing but agents of the colonial powers' given scientific status to justify European domination, and that those in power deliberately distorted the image of Africa.

He did not specify workers rather than colonised peoples as the ones exploited, so not +2.

property-franchise.rationale: Demanded the ballot for every Black American and said 'a man has a right to vote, a man has a right to be registered'; he did not discuss property qualifications specifically.

race-social-construct.rationale: In his January 1965 Harlem talk he argued that the racial categories of 'Mongoloid, Caucasoid and Negroid' were drawn by anthropologists acting as agents of colonial powers to justify domination, and that who counts as 'Negroid' was assigned inconsistently. The OAAU program calls 'racial' differences artificially created. He did not rule out biological claims in so many words.

racial-community-economic-control.rationale: Ballot or the Bullet states that the economic philosophy of Black nationalism 'only means that we should control the economy of our community', with Black people running the stores, banks and industry of their own community.

racial-franchise.rationale: Demanded that Black Americans get 'full use of the ballot in every one of the 50 states' and said anyone who stops people registering is breaking the law; the OAAU launched a voter registration drive.

racial-group-interests.rationale: The OAAU (June 1964) was open only to people of African descent, with whites invited to organise separately in the white community; its program states 'the exclusive ethnic quality of our unity is necessary for self-preservation' while saying it is 'not opposed to multiethnic associations'. Wikipedia reports he began to reconsider black nationalism in his last months, but no clear statement of that is in the sources used.

racial-oppression-before-sexism.rationale: No recorded position found in the sources read.

racial-pride.rationale: 'A race of people is like an individual man; until it uses its own talent, takes pride in its own history, expresses its own culture, affirms its own selfhood, it can never fulfill itself' (OAAU speech, June 1964); the program calls for a cultural revolution to restore identity.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Opposed legally enforced segregation: in Ballot or the Bullet he said he was against a segregated school system and demanded civil rights 'now', and the OAAU memorandum and program attack America for preaching integration while practising segregation. His own separation proposals of the Nation of Islam period were for voluntary separation and self-governance, not segregation by law.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: Stated throughout 1964-65 that racism in America was an 'incurable cancer' (Mecca letter) and the system a racist power structure that kept Black Americans in 'slavery' (OAAU program).

recall-officials.rationale: In the OAAU speech (June 1964) he said that 'any time the politician is not doing his job, we remove him', and supported only office-holders who answer to the Afro-American community. It is unclear whether he meant recall during a term or removal by election.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Same OAAU remarks (June 1964): support only for office-holders 'responsible to the Afro-American community' and removal of any who fail; the mechanism is not specified.
